A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOMOK framework despite the changed title. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original link-prediction experiments on four benchmarks, noise robustness tests, ablations, sensitivity analyses, and case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds missing-modality and sparse-link experiments, TuckER comparisons, and resource measurements.

M1.justification: ReMoKE, MuJoD, ExID, their training losses, alternating optimization, and inference score aggregation remain unchanged. Explicit relation subscripts and expanded CLUB explanations clarify the existing method rather than introduce a new procedure.

E1.justification: The four datasets and link-prediction task remain, but Section 5.4 expands DB15K evaluation from modality noise to missing modalities and sparse training links. These introduce two distinct information-availability scenarios, materially broadening robustness coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds TuckER as an evaluated baseline on all four datasets, increasing the comparison set from 19 to 20. TuckER was already cited and used as MOMOK's scoring function in v1. The robustness comparator set remains AdaMF, TBKGC, and QEB, also spelled QBE.

E3.justification: v2 adds random modality removal at plotted rates of 10–50%, training-triple removal at plotted sparse rates of 5–25%, and time/memory measurements. The original benchmark splits and named link-prediction metrics remain. Appendix B documents existing settings; it does not establish a changed training regime or rerun.

E4.justification: Figure 3 adds substantial tests of robustness to missing modality information and sparse links. New Section 5.6 and Table 4 examine computational cost against MMKRL, OTKGE, and MMRNS. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, and modality case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The newly explained averaging over head and tail predictions is not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds TuckER scores, missing-modality and sparse-link result curves, and resource measurements, including MOMOK's 9.8 seconds and 5900 MB in Table 4. All existing Table 2 scores and Table 3 ablations remain unchanged. TuckER becomes the strongest baseline on several metrics, but the improvement percentages are not updated: KVC16K Hit@1 values of 10.53 versus 9.79 imply about 7.6%, rather than the retained 23.0%.

T1.justification: v1 cites CLUB and states the implemented losses; v2 adds its general definition and Appendix A's two theorems and proofs concerning the upper bound and a KL-based condition for its variational approximation. This is substantial new mathematical content, although Equation 14 uses q-distribution expectations while Proof 2 proceeds with p-distribution expectations.

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims detailed theoretical justification as a contribution. The title and abstract emphasize entity representation learning, while the central claims about relation-guided experts, disentanglement, and strong MMKGC performance remain. No additional downstream task capability is demonstrated or established.

C2.justification: The robustness interpretation expands from noisy modalities to missing information and sparse links. Section 5.6 adds claims of manageable, linear computational overhead and favorable efficiency. The limitations concerning task specificity, lack of LLM integration, and medium-sized datasets are substantively unchanged, moving from Appendix A to C.

D1.justification: Appendix B and Table 6 newly disclose dataset-specific learning rates and embedding dimensions, plus 2000 training epochs and other selected hyperparameters. v1 primarily supplied tuning ranges. Hardware, software, and code/data access information remain unchanged; these additions improve documentation without establishing an implementation change.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion is shortened, and references to Wang et al.'s 2017 embedding survey, Pezeshkpour et al. (2018), and Liang et al. (2023) are removed. The opening positions the work more explicitly within entity representation learning. Most cited foundations remain; author-year citation formatting is a presentation change.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, rewrites the opening motivation and parts of the abstract, expands the CLUB explanation, and adds an efficiency research question and section. New analytical and experimental-detail appendices precede the retained limitations and impacts. Most existing methodological and results prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redesigned from two plots into a six-panel comparison with a shared legend. New efficiency and hyperparameter tables are added, while existing figures and tables are resized or relocated. The document also adopts substantially different title, heading, header, citation, and table formatting.

improvement.justification: The additional robustness scenarios, relevant TuckER comparison, and exact hyperparameters provide a limited net improvement in validation and reproducibility. Reporting defects constrain that gain: Table 2 and Section 5.3 retain outdated improvement margins, Appendix B.2's metric formulas omit the factor of two needed for head/tail averaging, and Appendix A's variational definition conflicts with its proof. The unchanged core results remain useful, but the additions require correction before supporting a substantial quality improvement.
